source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning - text editing
finding: DreamCoder learned a library and a recognition net on text-editing tasks. Held-out solve rate rose sharply after learning.
numbers: SyGuS text editing: 3.7% solved in 10 min (mean search 235 s) before learning, 79.6% after (mean 40 s). Best prior solver CVC4 got 82.4% at 1 hour and 8 CPUs per task; DreamCoder got 84.3% under that same budget.
limits: Narrow DSL programs; the big-budget comparison is only at the end.
agent_relevance: A wake-sleep loop can lift a weak searcher about 20x in solve rate on one domain. Shows the size of gain a subgoal library could give.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning - ablations across domains
finding: Both sleep phases matter. Removing library refactoring, removing the recognition net (dreaming), or memorising whole solutions instead of compressing all lowered held-out solve rate.
numbers: DreamCoder solved the most held-out tasks in every domain. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative passed 60% while DreamCoder reached nearly 100%. Mean solve time 54.1 s, median 15.0 s. Training to convergence about a day on 20-100 CPUs.
quote: each of DreamCoder's core components ... contributes substantively to its overall performance
limits: Training cost is large; domains are program synthesis.
agent_relevance: Store compressed reusable pieces, not raw past solutions, in the subgoal library. Matches the abstraction-sleep step.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning - physics and math laws
finding: Starting from generic list primitives (map, fold, arithmetic), DreamCoder rebuilt vector algebra and then physical laws over wake-sleep cycles.
numbers: After 8 wake/sleep cycles it learned 93% of 60 laws and identities from AP and MCAT physics cheat sheets (inner product, vector sum, norm first, then inverse-square law).
limits: Numeric example data given; tasks are equations, not open-ended reasoning.
agent_relevance: Library grows in layers: small pieces first, then pieces built on them. A hierarchy of subgoals, not a flat list.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning - compute cost
finding: The authors state the search is heavy; harder runs needed days on tens of CPUs.
numbers: Main domains about one day on 20-100 CPUs; one hard set solved all 20 problems after roughly five days on 64 CPUs.
limits: I did not confirm which problem set the 5-day run belongs to.
agent_relevance: This is the cost that LLM search later tried to remove (see LILO).

source: Wong, Ellis, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2021) LAPS: leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics
finding: Adding natural-language task descriptions to DreamCoder's loop improved library quality and search, even with no language at test time.
numbers: Held-out solved: strings 33.4% (DreamCoder) vs 52.2-57.0% (LAPS variants). Graphics (n=111) best 49.55% vs 98.19% (LAPS+ME+compression); mean 42.64 vs 81.98. Scenes 67.8% vs 95.6%. No language at test: LAPS library with enumeration 62.16% vs DreamCoder library 41.44% on graphics. Human-written language: 58.55% graphics vs 89.20% on synthetic test language.
limits: Big drop with real human language on graphics; seed spread large (best 92.79 vs mean 52.93 for LAPS in neural search).
agent_relevance: Language names for subgoals help both search and library quality. An LLM agent already has language to name each stored subgoal.

source: Grand, Wong, Bowers, Olausson, Liu, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2024) LILO: learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LILO swaps DreamCoder's enumerative search for an LLM solver, uses Stitch to compress, and has the LLM write names and docs for each abstraction (AutoDoc). Best overall.
numbers: Online test solve rate, mean of 3 runs: REGEX DreamCoder 43.93 / LLM Solver 76.13 / LILO 77.07; CLEVR 94.50 / 88.67 / 96.76; LOGO 28.53 / 32.13 / 48.95 (max 73.87). LILO minus DreamCoder: +33.14 REGEX, +2.26 CLEVR, +20.42 LOGO. One round of LLM synthesis costs about the dollar equivalent of 48 CPU-hours of DreamCoder search.
limits: Codex-era GPT model; large seed spread (LOGO std 9.46; REGEX LLM Solver std 12.04). Over the LLM Solver alone LILO adds only +0.94 on REGEX.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an LLM wake-sleep loop: solve, compress, document, reuse.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO - AutoDoc ablation
finding: Giving the LLM raw anonymous abstractions hurt. Adding LLM-written documentation recovered most of the loss.
numbers: Stitch abstractions without docs vs LLM Solver: -30.60 REGEX, -2.91 CLEVR, -11.11 LOGO. Adding AutoDoc: +9.73 REGEX, +2.27 CLEVR, +0.00 LOGO over the undocumented condition.
limits: LOGO got no gain from docs; authors blame semantic errors in the docs.
agent_relevance: Each stored subgoal needs a plain name, description and usage example. An unlabeled library can make the agent worse.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO - offline library quality
finding: Libraries learned in the loop work even without language help. Compression done in the loop beats compression done afterwards.
numbers: Offline enumerative synthesis with final library vs base DSL: DreamCoder +19.6 REGEX, +62.46 CLEVR, +29.73 LOGO; LILO +42.27, +63.43, +43.24. LILO library also beat libraries derived post-hoc from the LLM Solver runs.
limits: Tests the library only, with enumeration and no LLM.
agent_relevance: Grow the library inside the solving loop, not as a one-off clean-up at the end.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Stitch: top-down synthesis for library learning (POPL)
finding: Stitch finds the same kind of abstractions as DreamCoder's compression step far faster, by top-down pattern search over a corpus.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder's compression, with comparable or better compression. Early stopping costs little: near-best libraries within <2% of the compute on some domains.
limits: Measures compression, not downstream solve rate. Lambda-calculus DSL.
agent_relevance: Makes the abstraction-sleep step cheap enough to run every few tasks.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions (ICML)
finding: An LLM refactors solved programs into verified helper functions kept in a code bank. Weaker open models gain a lot from them.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B absolute gains: +11.5% LOGO, +26.1% Date, +8.1% TextCraft. Date: 45.6 primitive vs 57.1 ReGAL (13B); GPT-3.5 88.9 vs 90.2. TextCraft CodeLlama-34B 22.2 vs 30.8 (ReAct GPT-3.5 25.6). About 200 training examples. MATH +11.8% for GPT-3.5.
limits: Small gain for the strong model on Date (+1.3). Lemur-70B gave many empty outputs and baseline and ReGAL were roughly tied there.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to wake (solve), sleep (refactor and verify) on an LLM with no training.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL - component ablations
finding: Each part of the sleep step matters. Example ordering and the retry step matter most.
numbers: Dev accuracy, CodeLlama-13B, full ReGAL LOGO 55.0 / Date 77.0 / TextCraft 34.12. Without retry 48.3 / 51.9 / 30.43. Without curriculum (random order) 36.3 / 56.6 / 28.78 (-18.7 on LOGO). Without pruneCodeBank 52.0 / 65.5 / 25.26. Without editCodeBank 53.3 / 69.6 / 27.35.
limits: Dev splits only, one model; curriculum is shortest-query-first.
agent_relevance: Consolidate easy tasks first, verify each stored piece by running it, prune and edit the library.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes
finding: Training-free loop where the model creates, uses and periodically trims functions. Claimed higher accuracy with much smaller toolboxes.
numbers: 11 datasets; toolboxes 79-98% smaller than baselines; human verification 31% faster and 13% more accurate (abstract figures).
limits: Later reanalysis found reuse almost never happens in its MATH runs (next line).
agent_relevance: Trimming rarely used pieces keeps the library short and easy to check.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't - TroVE reanalysis
finding: Re-running TroVE on MATH shows learned functions are almost never reused. A no-reuse ablation does as well or better, so gains come from many sampled attempts.
numbers: Final library only 15 functions, covering 3 of 7 MATH subjects. Only 3 reuses in 3,201 test questions. No-reuse ablation vs reproduced (5 trials): counting 0.250 vs 0.236, number 0.290 vs 0.258, intermediate algebra 0.134 vs 0.120, geometry 0.050 vs 0.058. Reproduction within 2% of reported.
limits: Small open model (CodeLlama-7B); MATH only; import statements excluded.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication-style result: a library can look useful when self-consistency is the real driver. Measure reuse directly (G4).

source: Berlot-Attwell et al. (2024) Library learning doesn't - LEGO-Prover reanalysis
finding: In the LEGO-Prover logs, learned lemmas were almost never reused. Removing cross-problem sharing barely changed results.
numbers: Over 20,000 lemmas learned; 1,233 (6%) reached the prover input; exactly one reused verbatim, once; none reused more than once by name. Ablation without sharing (GPT-4o-mini, 12 problems, 50 attempts, 2 trials) solved only 1 problem fewer than baseline.
limits: Tiny ablation (12 problems); original used retired GPT-3.5 versions.
agent_relevance: Track reuse count per stored subgoal. A library with near-zero reuse is just extra prompt.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: An LLM agent in Minecraft keeps a skill library of verified code, retrieved by description. It learns across tasks with no weight updates.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech milestones up to 15.3x faster (wood 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x) than prior SOTA; only method to reach diamond. Without the skill library the tech tree row reads 7, 9, 29 iterations then N/A (0 of 3 runs) for the last tier.
limits: Needs GPT-4; authors say GPT-3.5 code was too weak. Success is judged by game state, a clean check.
agent_relevance: A wake-sleep style skill library works in an agent loop when each skill is verified before storing.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows from past tasks, offline from training data or online from its own test trajectories, and puts them in memory.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4, online): +12.0 absolute, +51.1% relative success over BrowserGym; +7.6% relative over SteP with human-written workflows; about 2.0 fewer steps per task. Mind2Web cross-task +24.6% relative step success. Online beats offline by growing margin as train/test gap widens (8.9-14.0 points over baselines). Workflow actions were called in only 18.5% of tasks when added as actions.
limits: Online workflows built from model-predicted success so wrong ones can enter; agents resist new actions.
agent_relevance: Self-supervised induction during use can beat offline induction when the test domain differs.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory
finding: Distils strategies from both successes and failures into memory items, retrieved at test time. Beats raw-trajectory and success-only memories.
numbers: WebArena overall success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 over no memory for three backbones; up to 20% relative gain, up to 16% fewer steps. First backbone: AWM 44.4 vs ReasoningBank 49.7 on one subset, 51.8 with memory-aware scaling in the overall column. Self-judge accuracy 72.7% against ground truth.
limits: Success labels come from the model and are wrong about 27% of the time; web and software tasks only.
agent_relevance: Learning from failures helps, but use code-checked labels instead of a self-judge (G2, G3).

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: A growing cheatsheet of strategies and code snippets carried across questions lifts accuracy when the model reuses code.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%; AIME 2025 +30; GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99% (DC-RS); GPQA-Diamond +9; MMLU-Pro Engineering and Physics up to +8. Claude Game of 24 only 12% to 14%. Claude 3.5 Haiku AIME 2024 10.0 to 26.7-36.7.
limits: Small models stall: memory fills with wrong attempts and retrieval is poor. Gain depends on the model choosing to reuse code.
agent_relevance: Shows both the upside and the failure mode: stored tricks help only if the solver uses them.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent collects experience, extracts natural-language insights and recalls similar successes. No weight updates.
numbers: ALFWorld: retrieve-only 40.3% to 54.4% over four rounds; ExpeL+Reflexion 54.5% to 60.4%. HotpotQA ExpeL about 40% vs Reflexion 39% without repeated attempts.
limits: On ALFWorld Reflexion alone still scores higher (59% vs 54%).
agent_relevance: Insight extraction (sleep) and example retrieval (wake) are separable gains; test each.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) CRAFT: creating and retrieving specialized toolsets
finding: Builds a verified toolset from solved training problems, abstracted into snippets, then retrieves them by multi-view matching.
numbers: Average 43.16% relative F1 gain over best baselines on vision-language tasks; performance keeps rising with more tools and stronger backbones.
limits: Gains depend on backbone strength; tools come from the same task family.
agent_relevance: Another solve, verify, abstract, retrieve loop; works best on narrow task families.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute: beyond inference scaling at test time
finding: The model thinks offline about a context before any question arrives and stores the notes. At question time it needs far less compute.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME (60 questions). Scaling sleep compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Amortised over many queries on one context: 2.5x lower cost per query. 5 parallel sleep generations beat 10.
limits: Needs questions predictable from context; o1 showed limited gains.
agent_relevance: LLM version of the sleep phase: precompute likely subgoals between tasks.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute - predictability
finding: How predictable a query is from its context, scored by log-probability under a base model, tracks how much sleep-time compute helps.
numbers: Predictable questions were simpler and gained more; unpredictable ones were more complex and gained less. Sleep-time compute generally Pareto-dominates pass@k at equal test-time tokens.
limits: Correlation from one dataset family; predictability scored with Llama2-70B.
agent_relevance: Run an offline sleep step only where the next task is predictable from what is stored.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou, Silver (2016) Prioritized experience replay
finding: Replaying surprising transitions more often speeds learning in deep RL.
numbers: Beat DQN with uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games.
limits: Prioritising adds bias that needs importance weights; Atari only.
agent_relevance: Older non-language replay; priority by surprise is a model for which memories to rehearse.

source: Shin, Lee, Kim, Kim (2017) Continual learning with deep generative replay
finding: A generator replays fake past data while a solver learns new tasks, inspired by hippocampal replay, reducing forgetting without stored real data.
numbers: Sequential MNIST solver reached about 98.5-98.8% on full test data; also tested on permuted-pixel tasks and an MNIST to SVHN domain shift where accuracy fell when shared parameters changed.
limits: Small image tasks; replay quality limits performance.
agent_relevance: Pseudo-rehearsal ancestor of the dream fantasies in DreamCoder's dreaming step.

source: Mnih et al. (2013) Playing Atari with deep reinforcement learning
finding: Introduced the experience replay buffer for deep Q-learning.
numbers: No numbers recorded; file not read this session.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Founding use of a replay buffer in AI.

source: Bornschein, Bengio (2015) Reweighted wake-sleep
finding: Improves Hinton's wake-sleep algorithm for deep generative models with importance weights.
numbers: No numbers recorded; only the title page was seen.
limits: Neural wake-sleep, not LLM.
agent_relevance: Background for the name wake-sleep.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Self-synthesized rehearsal (SSR)
finding: The model writes its own rehearsal data; refined and filtered; used in later fine-tuning to reduce forgetting.
numbers: Abstract states it matches or beats conventional rehearsal; no numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only; training-based, which our scaffold agent does not do.
agent_relevance: Pseudo-rehearsal for LLM weights; not usable in a scaffold-only agent.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: where DreamCoder-style loops help or fail with LLMs
finding: Strong gains where tasks share structure and a verifier exists (LOGO, REGEX, Minecraft, Game of 24, WebArena). Weak or null where reuse is rare (MATH, miniF2F).
numbers: Reuse: 3 of 3,201 (TroVE MATH); 1 of 20,000+ lemmas (LEGO-Prover). Gains with reuse: LILO +20.42 LOGO, ReGAL +26.1 Date (13B), DC 10% to 99% Game of 24.
limits: Different models and years; no study runs one loop across all domains.
agent_relevance: Keep a library only for task families with repeated structure; store verified items with a name and docs; track reuse per item.
